study.title: Psalm 72 The Righteous King, Peace and Blessing for All Nations
study.overview: This psalm presents a prayer for the king, asking God to grant him righteous judgment and righteousness. The expected result of this government is broad: protection for the poor, the end of oppression, lasting peace, fertility of the earth and influence that reaches the nations. At the same time, the psalm ends by raising the glory of God Himself, showing that the greatness of the king is always derived and subordinated to the Lord. In evangelical reading, the text points to the ideal reign that finds its full fulfillment in the Messiah, the Son of David.

outline.title: The King Needs to Receive God's Righteousness
outline.explanation: The opening asks God to give to the king his judgments and his righteousness. The focus is not on gross power, but a government, especially for the poor, of the afflicted and against the oppressor.

outline.title: The effect of fair government: peace and prosperity
outline.explanation: As long as the king lives under the blessing of God, the people fear the Lord and experience freshness, flourishing and continuous peace. The images of rain and abundance show that righteousness produces life and harmony.

outline.title: A broad domain with special care for those in need
outline.explanation: The king receives dominion of universal scope, with tribute from the nations and submission of kings. But his authority manifests itself in compassion: he saves the needy, protects the poor and considers the life of the afflicted precious.

outline.title: Blessing to the king, abundance on earth and final glory of God
outline.explanation: The psalm asks for prosperity, continuous honor and praise to the king, but concludes by redirecting the worship of the Lord, the only author of wonders. The final note closes David's prayers, marking a transition in the book of Psalms.

study.context: The title indicates a prayer for Solomon, that is, linked to the king of the lineage of David. The commentator notes note that the psalm closes the second book of the Psalter and functions as a kind of epilogue. There is also the idea that prayer targets the reality of Israel's monarchy, but goes beyond it, projecting a perfectly just government that goes beyond the common experience of human kings.
study.theology: The psalm unites three central themes: royalty, justice and universal blessing. The true king is not defined by conquest alone, but by righteousness, compassion, and defense of the weak. This shows that authority, in the biblical perspective, should reflect the righteous character of God. The peace described is not mere political silence; it is the fruit of justice applied wisely and mercifully. The reach of the sea and the accession of the nations suggest a hope that exceeds any merely earthly reign, pointing to the Messiah as the definitive king of David's lineage. In the end, however, the glory does not rest on the king itself, but in God, who is the only author of such wonders and whose honor must fill the whole earth.

scholarViews.insight: The comment notes that justice and dominion sought in prayer point to what is fully fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David.

The note presented connects the psalm to a broader editorial tradition, noting that it is part of a set of songs attributed in the headlines to Asafe or intended for him, according to the reading mentioned.
The comment understands the final phrase as the closure of David's prayers and as a transition milestone in the organization of the book.

questions: What kind of leadership does the psalm consider truly fair: what dominates or the one that protects the poor and afflicted?
How does the description of peace, fertility and joy show that biblical justice reaches all community life?
How does this psalm correct the temptation to seek human glory without recognizing that only God does wonders?
study.practice: Pray for rulers and authorities asking God to grant them justice, discernment and compassion. Also evaluate your own influence: at home, at work and in the church, does it serve to oppress or alleviate the needy? Apply the psalm seeking a posture of practical justice, generosity with the fragile and trust that true peace depends on righteousness before God.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided about Matthew Henry appear truncated and seem to deal with a broader section of the Psalter, not offering a clearly specific observation about all the verses of this chapter. Therefore, the pointing associated with him was done with caution, without enlarging beyond what the excerpt allows. It is also not possible to state safely, only from the notes given, all the historical details of the authorship and the occasion of the psalm.
